title: Disputed microfossils in the Nuvvuagittuq rocks
description: Tiny tubes and filaments of iron oxide in ancient seafloor rocks in Quebec were described in 2017 as fossil microbes from hydrothermal vents.
uncertainty: Doubly uncertain: different dating methods put the rocks anywhere from about 3.77 to about 4.3 billion years old, and the structures may have formed without life.

title: Possible trace of life in Jack Hills zircon
description: Graphite sealed inside a 4.1-billion-year-old zircon crystal has a carbon isotope ratio of the kind living things produce. It is the oldest claimed chemical hint of life.
uncertainty: Disputed: it rests on a single mineral grain, and non-biological processes can produce similar carbon ratios.

title: Possible traces of life at Isua
description: Rocks in south-west Greenland contain graphite with a carbon signature typical of life, and in 2016 layered structures there were reported as fossil microbial mats (stromatolites).
uncertainty: Disputed: a 2018 study argued the layered structures were made by deformation of the rock, and the carbon evidence is also debated; the belt is 3.7 to 3.8 billion years old.

title: Oldest widely accepted fossils
description: Layered mounds built by mats of microbes (stromatolites) are preserved in cherts of the Pilbara region, in the Dresser Formation and the slightly younger Strelley Pool Formation. They are the oldest evidence of life that most researchers accept.
uncertainty: The Dresser Formation is dated to 3.48 billion years and Strelley Pool to about 3.43 billion; some individual microfossil claims from the Pilbara (the Apex chert) remain contested.

title: Photosynthesis and cyanobacteria
description: Microbes learned to capture sunlight, first without releasing oxygen, and later cyanobacteria evolved the oxygen-releasing form that plants still use. Fossil filaments about 3.4 billion years old are thought to be photosynthetic, and oxygen-producing cyanobacteria must have existed before oxygen built up in the air.
uncertainty: Poorly constrained: oxygen-producing photosynthesis must predate the rise of oxygen at least 2.45 to 2.32 billion years ago, but how much earlier is debated, and firm cyanobacterial fossils go back only about 2.1 billion years.

title: First eukaryotes
description: Cells with a nucleus and internal compartments, the kind that make up all animals, plants and fungi, appear in the fossil record. Microfossils from North China about 1.65 billion years old are among the oldest generally accepted examples.
uncertainty: Estimates range widely: possible fossils such as Grypania are as old as 2.1 billion years, a molecular-clock study puts a key eukaryote trait at 2.3 billion years, and the oldest reliable chemical traces are only about 800 million years old.

title: Early large multicellular organisms
description: Fossils around ten centimetres in scale from the Gaoyuzhuang Formation in North China show organisms built of many cells. Multicellular life evolved independently at least 25 times among eukaryotes.
uncertainty: The 2.1-billion-year-old Francevillian structures from Gabon have been proposed as older multicellular life, but whether they are fossils at all is debated.

title: Bangiomorpha, the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction
description: Bangiomorpha, a fossil red alga from Arctic Canada, has distinct reproductive cells and is the oldest known organism that reproduced sexually. It is also the oldest fossil that can be placed in a living group.
uncertainty: The age of 1,047 million years comes from a 2017 dating study of the rocks; this is the oldest fossil evidence of sex, not necessarily its origin.

title: The Ediacaran biota
description: Large, soft-bodied organisms spread across the sea floor, known from sites such as Mistaken Point in Newfoundland, the Ediacara Hills in Australia and the White Sea. Dickinsonia, one of the best known, left traces of cholesterol, which points to an animal, though fungi or red algae are not excluded.
uncertainty: The first forms appeared around 600 million years ago and diversified from about 575 million; what kind of organisms most of them were is still debated.

title: The Cambrian explosion
description: Within a geologically short time most of the major animal groups alive today appeared in the fossil record, many with shells, limbs and eyes. It is known from exceptionally preserved fossil beds such as Chengjiang and the Burgess Shale.
uncertainty: The start is tied to the base of the Cambrian at 538.8 million years; the burst is estimated to have lasted 13 to 25 million years.

title: Chengjiang fossils and the first vertebrates
description: The Chengjiang fossil beds of Yunnan preserve soft-bodied animals from early in the Cambrian explosion, including Haikouichthys, a small fish-like animal regarded as one of the earliest known vertebrates.
uncertainty: Whether Haikouichthys is a true vertebrate or a close relative on the vertebrate stem is debated.

title: The Burgess Shale
description: Mudslides in a Cambrian sea buried animals so quickly that soft parts were preserved in the Burgess Shale of the Canadian Rockies. The fossils give a detailed picture of early animal communities.

title: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification
description: Marine life diversified greatly: the number of orders of sea animals doubled and families tripled, and reefs and plankton communities became much richer.
uncertainty: The limits are a matter of definition; the figures here follow one recent estimate, and other authors place the main pulse later in the Ordovician.

title: Plants colonise the land
description: The first land plants, small relatives of mosses and liverworts, spread onto the continents. The earliest evidence is fossil spores from the middle Ordovician; plants with water-conducting tissue such as Cooksonia follow in the Silurian.
uncertainty: The date is that of the oldest spores; molecular estimates of the origin of land plants are earlier, from about half a billion years ago and in some studies far older.

title: End-Ordovician mass extinction
description: The first of the five great mass extinctions removed about 85 percent of marine species, in pulses linked to a sudden glaciation over the southern continent Gondwana.
uncertainty: The International Commission on Stratigraphy dates the end of the Ordovician to 443.1 million years, give or take 0.9 million; species-loss percentages are statistical estimates.

title: First jawed fish
description: Vertebrates with jaws appear in the fossil record. The oldest unambiguous remains are Qianodus and Fanjingshania from early Silurian rocks of Guizhou, China.
uncertainty: Isolated scales from the Late Ordovician may belong to jawed fish and would push the origin earlier.

title: Arthropods breathe air on land
description: The millipede Pneumodesmus, found near Stonehaven in Scotland, has breathing openings that could only work in air, making it one of the earliest known land animals.
uncertainty: First dated to about 428 million years (Silurian); a 2017 zircon study gave about 414 million years (Early Devonian), and the age is still discussed.

title: First forests
description: Trees evolved and formed the first forests. Fossil stumps at Gilboa in New York State belong to Wattieza, a tree at least 8 metres tall and the earliest known.
uncertainty: The age is approximate (Middle Devonian).

title: Tiktaalik and the move onto land
description: Tiktaalik, a fish from Arctic Canada with a flat head, a neck and sturdy fins containing limb-like bones, shows how four-limbed animals (tetrapods) arose from fish.
uncertainty: Its age has been reported as 375, 379 and 383 million years, and trackways from Poland about 12 million years older suggest tetrapods already existed, so Tiktaalik was a late survivor of the transition rather than the ancestor.
place: Fram Formation, Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, Canada

title: Late Devonian mass extinction
description: A series of extinction pulses hit life in the seas, especially reef builders. The main one, the Kellwasser event, falls at the boundary between the Frasnian and Famennian ages; a second, the Hangenberg event, closed the Devonian.
uncertainty: Dates are the ICS boundaries (372.15 and 358.86 million years); losses are estimated at around 40 percent of marine species in the main pulse, and the causes (ocean oxygen loss, cooling, volcanism) are debated.

title: The Carboniferous coal forests
description: Vast swamp forests of giant clubmosses and other seedless plants covered the tropical lowlands. Their buried remains became much of the world's coal, which gives the Carboniferous its name.
uncertainty: These are the limits of the Carboniferous Period as given by the source; the ICS now dates them to 358.86 and 298.9 million years.

title: Insects take to the air
description: Insects became the first animals to fly. The oldest winged insect fossils, such as Delitzschala, come from the early part of the Carboniferous.
uncertainty: The origin of wings is not preserved in the fossil record; an Early Devonian fossil, Rhyniognatha, is older, but it is uncertain whether it had wings or was even an insect.

title: First amniotes
description: Animals that lay shelled eggs on land, the group that includes reptiles, birds and mammals, appear. Hylonomus, found inside fossil tree stumps at Joggins, has long been regarded as the earliest known reptile.
uncertainty: A 2025 analysis placed Hylonomus just outside the amniotes proper, and clawed footprints from Australia dated to 358.9 to 354 million years ago suggest the group arose considerably earlier.

title: End-Permian mass extinction
description: The largest extinction known: about 81 percent of marine species and 70 percent of land vertebrate species died out. The main cause was the huge volcanic eruptions that formed the Siberian Traps.
uncertainty: Dated very precisely, between 251.941 and 251.880 million years ago; the percentages are estimates.

title: First dinosaurs
description: The oldest dinosaurs known from substantial remains come from Late Triassic rocks of southern Brazil (Santa Maria Formation, 233 million years) and Argentina (Ischigualasto Formation, 231 to 230 million years), where Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus were found.
uncertainty: Dinosaurs may be older: Nyasasaurus, about 243 million years old, could be one, but its remains are too fragmentary to be sure.

title: First mammals
description: Small, shrew-like early mammals such as Morganucodon appear in the Late Triassic, living alongside the first dinosaurs.
uncertainty: The answer depends on where the line is drawn between mammals and their close relatives; the oldest known member of a living mammal group, Juramaia, is about 160 million years old.

title: End-Triassic mass extinction
description: An extinction at the Triassic-Jurassic boundary removed about 23 to 34 percent of marine genera and many land animals, clearing the way for dinosaurs to dominate. It is generally attributed to eruptions of the Central Atlantic magmatic province.
uncertainty: The boundary is dated to 201.4 million years, give or take 0.2 million; loss estimates vary between studies.

title: Archaeopteryx and the first birds
description: Archaeopteryx, from the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, combined feathered wings with teeth, claws and a bony tail, linking birds to dinosaurs.
uncertainty: It was long counted as the oldest bird, but older feathered relatives such as Anchiornis, Xiaotingia and Aurornis have since been found, and where to draw the line for 'bird' is debated.

title: First flowering plants
description: Flowering plants appear in the fossil record in the Early Cretaceous and diversify quickly; by the Late Cretaceous they dominated many landscapes.
uncertainty: Fossils fix their appearance at about 130 million years, but the lineage leading to them is much older according to molecular evidence, and a few claimed earlier fossil flowers are disputed.

title: End-Cretaceous mass extinction
description: An asteroid 10 to 15 kilometres wide struck at Chicxulub in Mexico, and about three quarters of all species died out, including all dinosaurs other than birds, the pterosaurs, the large marine reptiles and the ammonites.
uncertainty: The ICS dates the boundary to 66.0 million years; how much the Deccan Traps eruptions contributed is debated.

title: Early primates
description: The first primates or their closest relatives appear soon after the dinosaur extinction. Purgatorius, as old as 66 million years, is among the earliest primate-like mammals.
uncertainty: Whether Purgatorius is a primate or a near relative is debated, and genetic estimates of when primates split from other mammals range from about 85 to about 55 million years.

title: Grasses and grasslands spread
description: Grasses, the last major plant group to rise to importance, became significant from around 40 million years ago, and open grasslands later replaced forest over large areas, reshaping grazing animals.
uncertainty: Grasses themselves go back to the Late Cretaceous; the timing of true grasslands differs by continent, with some sources placing the first ones only about 5 million years ago.

title: Sahelanthropus, a possible first hominin
description: A skull found in Chad in 2001 may belong to the oldest known member of the human lineage after its split from the chimpanzee lineage. The position of the opening for the spinal cord suggests an upright posture.
uncertainty: Disputed: studies of a thigh bone disagree on whether it walked upright, and some researchers do not accept it as a hominin.

title: Ardipithecus ramidus
description: The partial skeleton known as 'Ardi', from the Middle Awash in Ethiopia, shows an early hominin that could walk upright but still had a grasping big toe for climbing.

title: First stone tools
description: The oldest known stone tools are large flaked stones from Lomekwi, west of Lake Turkana, dated to 3.3 million years by their position between volcanic ash layers. The more widespread Oldowan toolkit appears by about 2.9 million years ago at Nyayanga, Kenya, and 2.6 million years ago at Gona, Ethiopia.
uncertainty: Lomekwi is a single site, dated indirectly from its position in the sediments; Oldowan tools are known from many sites.

title: 'Lucy' and Australopithecus afarensis
description: Lucy, a partial skeleton of an adult female found at Hadar in 1974, showed that hominins walked upright long before brains grew large. Her species lived in eastern Africa between about 3.85 and 2.95 million years ago.

title: The genus Homo
description: A lower jaw from Ledi-Geraru in Ethiopia, dated to 2.75 to 2.8 million years, is the earliest known fossil of our own genus. Homo habilis is known from about 2.4 million years ago.
uncertainty: The jaw is a single fragment and its assignment to Homo rests on tooth and jaw shape.

title: Homo erectus leaves Africa
description: Skulls and stone tools at Dmanisi in Georgia are the earliest well-dated hominin fossils outside Africa. Homo erectus went on to reach China and Indonesia.
uncertainty: Dmanisi is the oldest confirmed site outside Africa; possible stone tools from Shangchen in China have been tentatively dated to as much as 2.12 million years.

title: Control of fire
description: Early humans began to use and later to make fire. Burnt bone deep inside Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa (between 1.79 and 1.07 million years old) and heated sediment at Koobi Fora in Kenya (1.5 million years) point to use of fire by Homo erectus, and cooking is indicated at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in Israel about 780,000 years ago.
uncertainty: Claims range back to 2 million years ago, and early traces are hard to tell from natural fires; evidence only becomes common and convincing 400,000 to 300,000 years ago.

title: Neanderthals
description: Neanderthals lived across Europe and south-western to central Asia. They interbred with modern humans, and people outside Africa still carry some of their DNA.
uncertainty: Both ends are approximate: the lineage emerged gradually, and the last populations disappeared by about 40,000 years ago.

title: Homo sapiens
description: The oldest known fossils of our species come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, dated to about 315,000 years ago from burnt flint tools found with them. The Omo Kibish remains from Ethiopia, at least 233,000 years old, are the oldest in eastern Africa.
uncertainty: The Jebel Irhoud date is 315,000 years give or take 34,000 (a tooth gave 286,000 give or take 32,000), and the skulls mix modern faces with a more archaic braincase.

title: Early art and symbolic behaviour
description: At Blombos Cave in South Africa people mixed ochre pigment in shell containers about 100,000 years ago, and later engraved ochre, made shell beads and drew a cross-hatched pattern on stone 73,000 years ago. Cave paintings of animals in Sulawesi, Indonesia, are at least 45,500 years old.
uncertainty: When 'modern' behaviour began is debated and it probably emerged gradually; a hand stencil in Indonesia has been claimed to be at least 67,800 years old.

title: Modern humans spread out of Africa
description: People living outside Africa today descend mainly from a single expansion out of Africa in this period, as shown by genetic studies and fossils.
uncertainty: Earlier groups left Africa but contributed little to later populations: fossils in Israel date to 120,000 to 80,000 years and possibly about 185,000 years, and a skull fragment from Greece has been dated to 210,000 years.

title: People reach Australia
description: Modern humans crossed the sea to the ancient continent that joined Australia and New Guinea. Stone tools and ochre at the Madjedbebe rock shelter have been dated to about 65,000 years ago.
uncertainty: The Madjedbebe date (59,300 to 70,700 years) has been challenged as a possible effect of termites moving artefacts through the sand; about 50,000 years is the more conservative figure.

title: Modern humans in Europe
description: Bones and a tooth of Homo sapiens from Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria, about 46,000 years old, are among the oldest directly dated remains of modern humans in Europe. Neanderthals disappeared within a few thousand years.
uncertainty: A 2022 study of Grotte Mandrin in France argued for an earlier presence about 54,000 years ago, which is not yet confirmed.

title: People in the Americas
description: Human footprints preserved beside an ancient lake at White Sands, New Mexico, are the oldest firm evidence of people in the Americas, showing they were there during the height of the last ice age.
uncertainty: The first dates, from seeds of a water plant, were challenged as possibly too old; later dating of pollen and of quartz grains gave matching ages, though some researchers remain unconvinced.
place: White Sands National Park, New Mexico, United States
